**Proven cause: model logos are inferred only from the terminal title—not Pi’s model metadata. Pi 1.0.4’s default title does not include its model.**

- **Live evidence:** Alghul’s Pi pane `w1:p1` has the Pi agent-logo token (`E1A9`), no model-family match in its title, and neither `model` nor `model_stale` token. Darkseid’s three Hermes panes contain GPT/Claude family names in their titles and carry the corresponding model-logo tokens (`E1AF`/`E1A0`).
- **Exact failing boundary:** `lib/state.js:288–307` builds the agent entry from agent identity and terminal title; `:475` calls `modelFor(entry.title, entry.name)`. `lib/logos.js:247–261` matches family regexes against that title; fallback covers only Claude, Codex and Gemini—not Pi or Hermes. Therefore Pi’s model resolves to `null`. `lib/state.js:591–593` then clears both model tokens.
- **Backend → rendering:** Herdr’s `agent.list` supplies the title (`lib/herdr.js:139–140`); computed tokens are published through `pane.report_metadata` (`:228–235`). Sidebar configuration already renders `$model` and `$model_stale` beside the agent logo (`lib/managed-config.js:452–456`). The loss occurs **before rendering**, not in the glyph mapping.
- **Pi schema checked:** installed Pi is **1.0.4 on both hosts**. Its default title uses session name/cwd, without model (`dist/modes/interactive/interactive-mode.js:810–817`). Model metadata exists separately: `ModelChangeEntry` has `provider`/`modelId` (`dist/core/session-manager.d.ts:31–35`); `model_select` events expose `model`, `previousModel`, and `source` (`dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts:848–854`). Radar currently consumes neither.
- **Reproduction:** read-only Node check returned `null` family/glyph for `Pi - project`; adding `gpt-6.1-sol` to the sanitized title returned family `gpt` and glyph `✺`. Hermes without a model in its title also returned `null`.
- **Build/history:** both repositories are clean at `e258108`. Running daemons point to these repositories; SHA-256 hashes of all three relevant modules match across hosts. Alghul’s mounted daemon path resolves to its repo symlink. No on-disk build mismatch found. Model-logo logic originated in commit `292b189` on September 27, 2026.
- **Logs:** inspected bounded Herdr log tails on both hosts; no model mentions or `ERROR` lines. No visual/CDP inspection performed, so **no visual-pass claim**.

**Minimal fix required:** provide Pi’s selected model to the existing family mapper—either through explicit model metadata, or a Pi title hook that includes the model and updates on selection/restoration. Do not hardcode Pi to a provider; it supports multiple model families.

**Remaining uncertainty:** did not inspect active-session model records or custom Pi extensions, so the actual selected Pi model/provider remains unverified. Live missing-token behavior and the title-only detection defect are established.

**Changes:** none. No session contents, credentials, inference, restarts, installs, commits, or new sessions.

7|
8|# Skill: Write Specifications
9|
10|Use this skill before writing any new document that directs execution. This includes scopes, block
11|specs, plans, ADRs, handovers, and source-of-truth requirements. Use
12|`skill-amend-specs.md` instead when changing an existing contract in response to findings.
13|
14|A specification is ready only when an engineer can execute it without inventing product behavior,
15|guessing facts, choosing omitted requirements, or weakening verification.
16|
17|## Non-negotiable rules
18|
19|1. **Recover the whole mandate.** Preserve every obligation in the operator's request. Do not scope
20|   from a summary when the original wording is available.
21|2. **Discover facts; ask for decisions.** Read code, docs, APIs, and current system state yourself.
22|   Ask the operator only for genuine choices that evidence cannot settle.
23|3. **Ask one decision at a time.** Lead with the question, recommend one answer, and explain only
24|   the material trade-off.
25|4. **Never invent authority.** User-facing behavior, workflow, cost, destructive action, and scope
26|   changes require an operator decision unless already stated in the mandate.
27|5. **No hidden uncertainty.** A READY specification has no unanswered requirement question,
28|   unsupported factual claim, placeholder, or implied acceptance criterion.
29|6. **Verification is part of the requirement.** Every acceptance criterion names one observable
30|   method: `test:`, `cmd:`, `screenshot:`, or `manual_by:`.
31|7. **Prefer the smallest sufficient design.** Reuse existing components, conventions, and skills.
32|   Do not add future-proofing without a present requirement.
33|
34|## Workflow
35|
36|### 1. Build the obligation ledger
37|
38|Read the operator request and every inherited contract in full. Create one row per obligation:
39|
40|| ID | Source wording or reference | Required outcome | Destination | Status |
41||:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
42|
43|Use `captured`, `resolved`, or `blocked` for Status. Never drop an obligation because an existing
44|acceptance row looks similar. A final sweep must account for every row.
45|
46|### 2. Establish ground truth
47|
48|Inspect the current implementation and the documents that own the affected behavior. Search for
49|existing patterns before proposing a new one. For external APIs or libraries, read current official
50|documentation and record the version or retrieval date.
51|
52|Maintain an evidence ledger while researching:
53|
54|| Claim | Source | Observed evidence | Status |
55||:--|:--|:--|:--|
56|
57|Use `verified`, `contradicted`, or `unknown`. Do not write an `unknown` claim as fact. Do not ask the
58|operator to confirm a fact that can be discovered.
59|
60|### 3. Resolve decisions before drafting
61|
62|Separate unresolved items into:
63|
64|- **Facts:** investigate them.
65|- **Operator decisions:** ask one at a time with a recommendation.
66|- **Implementation details inside approved scope:** choose the simplest evidence-backed option.
67|- **Blocked unknowns:** define a spike or stop; do not disguise them as assumptions.
68|
69|Do not mark the specification READY while any operator decision or execution-critical fact remains
70|open. A blocked draft may list the unresolved item and what clears it; it is not an execution handoff.
71|
72|### 4. Bound the work
73|
74|State all applicable items explicitly:
75|
76|- problem, goal, actors, and current behavior
77|- target behavior and end-to-end happy path
78|- in-scope outcomes and named out-of-scope exclusions
79|- authority already granted and decisions still reserved to the operator
80|- prerequisites, dependencies, constraints, and compatibility requirements
81|- assumptions, each with evidence or a validation step
82|- affected repositories, modules, interfaces, data, and documents
83|- security, privacy, cost, deployment, and operational impact
84|- failure behavior, degraded behavior, recovery, rollback, and observability
85|- ordering constraints and independently verifiable delivery slices
86|
87|Write `none` where a required field genuinely has no entries. A blank section is an unanswered
88|question.
89|
90|### 5. Define requirements and verification
91|
92|Give every requirement a stable ID. For each requirement, write:
93|
94|- one observable outcome, not an implementation activity
95|- relevant actor, trigger, precondition, and expected result
96|- edge and failure behavior where applicable
97|- one acceptance criterion with its fixed verification method
98|- the evidence or operator decision that authorized it
99|
100|Use `manual_by:` only for irreducibly human judgment. Never replace a runnable check with manual
101|review because the check is inconvenient. Commands must name their working directory and must be
102|valid for the repository that will run them.
103|
104|### 6. Trace delivery
105|
106|Create a traceability table before handoff:
107|
108|| Requirement | Evidence / decision | Delivery task | Verification | Status |
109||:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
110|
111|Every requirement maps to at least one delivery task and one verification method. Every task maps
112|back to a requirement. Remove orphan tasks; add missing tasks.
113|
114|### 7. Run the adversarial sweep
115|
116|Re-read the whole specification, not only the latest diff. Check:
117|
118|- every obligation-ledger row is resolved
119|- every number, version, path, command, and cross-reference was verified at its source
120|- terminology is consistent and every actor is named
121|- scope does not widen or narrow the mandate
122|- no acceptance criterion says only "works", "correct", "handled", or equivalent
123|- happy path, failure path, recovery, and rollback do not contradict each other
124|- dependencies and ordering form an executable sequence
125|- the work fits the project's sizing limits; oversized work is split by deployable outcome
126|- no existing capability is being rebuilt without evidence that reuse fails
127|- no operator decision is hidden as an implementation detail or assumption
128|
129|Fix the class of defect, not only the first instance found.
130|
131|### 8. Issue the readiness verdict
132|
133|Use exactly one verdict:
134|
135|- **READY:** all obligations, facts, decisions, requirements, tasks, and checks are traceable and
136|  execution can begin without invention.
137|- **BLOCKED:** name the single next unresolved decision or evidence gap and what clears it. Do not
138|  dispatch execution.
139|
140|## Required handoff
141|
142|Return the specification path, verdict, obligation count, requirement count, and verification count.
143|For READY, all three counts must reconcile through the traceability table. For BLOCKED, ask only the
144|single next decision.
145|
146|## Reference examples
147|
148|Read `write-specs/examples.md` when drafting or reviewing the first specification in a session.
149|It contains a happy path, a safety-critical variant, and an anti-pattern with its correction.
150|
151|## Failure handling
152|
153|- Conflicting sources: cite both, mark BLOCKED, and ask which authority wins.
154|- Missing access or unavailable dependency: mark BLOCKED and name what access or evidence is needed.
155|- Multiple valid product interpretations: recommend one and ask the operator to choose.
156|- Review findings on an existing contract: stop this workflow and use `skill-amend-specs.md`.

# Dispatching Reviewer Subagents

Use this whenever you spawn a CLI coding agent to produce an independent review of a spec, PR, or
code, especially when the review may come back needing revision.

## Confirm authorization before any dispatch

Dispatch only when the operator explicitly asks for a review or the specific task's approved workflow expressly requires one. An instruction to monitor CI, merge when green, clean up, or close a session is not review authorization; do not convert a prerequisite check into an unsolicited reviewer call. If a required independent verdict is missing, report that gate concisely and ask for the needed decision without starting a reviewer or making adjacent edits. A dispatched review is a separate action, not an automatic consequence of seeing a PR.

## Dispatch one reviewer and keep its session

Treat a request for *a reviewer* as one reviewer and one model, even for high-risk work; do not add a second review from a default escalation policy when the operator specified the count or model. Before dispatch, pin the exact PR head/base and identify any in-scope uncommitted edits separately. If the verdict is incomplete or a factual claim needs correction, send a follow-up to the SAME CLI session with the exact missing paths/criteria; do not launch another reviewer or accept an informal verdict. Verify the process is actually stopped before saying it is stopped. Ensure the chosen CLI supports resume before launch.

When the operator explicitly asks for "another" or "a fresh" independent reviewer with "no biased info"/"no assumptions" after a prior round already found gaps, that IS a new, separately authorized dispatch (not the same-round follow-up rule above) — but the new subagent's context must contain ONLY the raw artifacts to inspect (PR numbers, repo paths, what claim is being verified), never the prior reviewer's findings, your own summary of them, or any framing of what was already fixed. State explicitly in its goal that it must search/read from scratch and form its own classification of each finding, not confirm or extend someone else's list. This is what makes the second opinion actually independent rather than an anchored rerun of the first.

## Default launcher: Hermes `delegate_task`

Use Hermes's built-in `delegate_task` by default, except when the operator requires incomplete work to return to the same agent/session: choose a resumable CLI before launch, because a completed delegate cannot satisfy that continuation requirement. An explicitly named launcher still takes precedence. Before using an external CLI, check its login once and inspect its execution/resume help; then verify access through the actual reviewer session without starting a second reviewer. Operator shorthand "gpt-sol" means Codex `-m gpt-5.6-sol`. For Codex progress, parse its `--json` events for completed items rather than applying a Hermes transcript pattern. When a new round starts, stop the previous watcher so stale heartbeats do not masquerade as current activity. Steer messages to a running delegate arrive only after its current tool call ends; do not promise an instantaneous response.

## Select and verify the requested model

Pass the operator's explicit model ID to the CLI; it overrides default model pools and escalation. When only one reviewer is authorized, do not spawn a separate model for a smoke test: check the CLI's model selection syntax, launch the single reviewer, then verify its reported model in that session's structured result before accepting its review. A rejected model or silent substitution blocks the review; do not pick a replacement without direction.

When the operator reports an existing working login, compare the launcher's configuration, inherited endpoint and supported credential source with that working setup before requesting authentication again. Use the CLI's authorized credential-loading mechanism; never dump secrets or repair credential stores as part of a review dispatch. Confirm access through the actual reviewer session, not an authentication-status probe alone. A failed launch is not a review round: do not print placeholder severity counts or a findings table before a review actually returns.

## Enforce read-only and protect secrets structurally

Constrain the CLI to Read/Glob/Grep and only the read-only Git/GitHub shell forms needed for the review; prose alone cannot prevent a Bash tool from reading credentials or changing state. Do not use a *plan* permission mode if the CLI treats it as an implementation-planning task and refuses a review; use a compatible read-only sandbox or narrow tool allowlist instead. Never grant broad shell access for production-config/variable commands, or ask the reviewer to dump environment JSON: these endpoints can print live secrets into the model transcript even when the intended field is only a branch. Supply a sanitized source-branch/deployment summary from the parent and label it parent-provided evidence. If a secret is exposed, stop further reads, never print its value while inspecting the transcript, alert the operator about rotation, and continue only within the same restricted session if the review remains authorized.

Before launch, map mandatory review steps to the restricted toolset. If the review skill requires current primary-source checks for external facts, allow public documentation fetches scoped to the needed domains (for Claude, `--tools Read,Glob,Grep,WebFetch` with `--allowedTools 'Read,Glob,Grep,WebFetch(domain:<official-domain>)'`). Keep production APIs, private data and unrelated network access excluded. Read-only must not mean denying the evidence access required for a valid verdict.

## Pack the evidence before launch

For manuscript work, complete the author's subtractive self-review before the next authorized independent review: remove repeated evidence, defensive review-response prose and unsupported implications; preserve sound passages, source qualifications and substantive disagreements. Then check each factual sentence against its source for actor, nested attribution, scope, action status and deadline semantics; check each inference for conditions the source does not establish. A clean voice check does not replace this evidence pass. Keep internal cutoff wording and publication-time rechecks in editorial notes; retain any date or qualification the reader needs to understand the claim. Measure before and after with the same counting method rather than comparing incompatible historical totals. Record this as author checking, never independent approval; exclude that record from the reviewer packet.

When the operator says "same principles", carry forward the requested model, neutral-input rules, full-source coverage and time cap without asking them to restate these. Apply subsequent cap or monitoring corrections before launch: update both the brief and external watchdog, not just the acknowledgement. Package the current revision, not the previous review's snapshot, and do not carry forward its findings into a fresh unbiased review. When reusing a packet, replace the complete manuscript block, recompute manuscript and source-file hashes, and inspect retained context for embedded prior verdicts; changing only the launcher can silently review an obsolete revision.

A read-only sandbox usually has no network and no session history, so hand the reviewer a
parent-provided evidence directory instead of letting it guess: the operator's messages verbatim
(pulled from session history, tool output excluded — the reviewer must map obligations from the
source, not the spec's own ledger), raw read-only `gh` outputs the spec cites, and every external
primary source the spec cites, fetched today with an access timestamp. Gitleaks-scan the directory
before launch. If the spec's tables hold commands, state in the brief that `\|` in a table cell is
GFM's escaped pipe and must be read as `|` when running the command; otherwise the reviewer runs the
raw markdown, its regexes match nothing, and it files a false finding. When the operator answered decisions tersely ("I click", "it's ok", "approved"),
pack the assistant question each answer replied to, verbatim and labelled; user-only messages make
every such decision look unrecoverable and the reviewer will rightly raise a BLOCKER. For an unbiased manuscript review, supply the exact current body and references, the report outline and editorial guidelines, adjacent-section text, voice requirements and source material. Exclude author recommendation memos, self-assessment, evidence-status verdicts and prior findings from the neutral packet; these can anchor the reviewer even when embedded inside the draft file. Retain factual provenance and access limitations, including which supplied sources are excerpts rather than complete texts. Label adjacent prose as context, not an additional review target, and label provisional length budgets as provisional. Check the assigned article against available neighbouring material; do not turn missing contributions into a requirement to finish or wait for the whole report. Distinguish article-only typesetting from assembled-report pagination, and never derive a subsection minimum from a report-wide page budget. Record both the exact supplied body-and-references hash and the source-file hash when editorial notes are stripped; otherwise the review cannot be tied unambiguously to the supplied revision.

Brief template and launch commands: `references/reviewer-brief-and-launch.md`.

## Run in background; audit completeness before acceptance

Launch the one CLI session as a notified background process and capture its structured final result, model and session ID. After exit, independently compare the reviewer's per-path inventory with the live changed-file manifests, including deleted files and explicitly scoped local edits; enumerate every obligation, requirement, and acceptance criterion rather than trusting a declared total. A grep-only or unread file is not reviewed. If any path/pass is missing, resume the SAME session with the specific remainder and do not call its BLOCKED/APPROVED text a complete review. Recover the verdict from structured output; do not open raw CLI transcripts when they may contain secrets. Distinguish review completeness from approval, CI success, mergeability, and later deployment validation. When asked for review errors, lead with demonstrated code defects and their severity; separately name any unfinished review checks. If no defects were reported but mandatory coverage is missing, say both plainly: no reported defects, review unaccepted. Do not describe timeout, incomplete coverage, or failed launch as a code finding, and do not present a provisional PASS as accepted approval. Keep this status answer to the requested errors rather than replaying dispatch history. When asked whether a reviewed spec is ready to merge and hand off, check its working-tree state, branch, PR and required checks before answering. State any remaining commit/PR/check/merge steps explicitly: a PASS on an uncommitted worktree is review approval, not merge readiness. Treat that readiness question as advice, not authorization to commit, merge, close the session or dispatch implementation.

When the operator's instruction DOES authorize merging (e.g. "merge/ship"), before calling the merge: confirm the PR's `headRefOid` equals the SHA you just pushed (uncommitted amendments from a review round are easy to leave unpushed); check branch protection for required status-check contexts (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/branches/<base>/protection`) and wait for that exact context to report success on the exact head SHA (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/status` or `check-runs`) rather than assuming a prior green run still applies; and clear any "DO NOT MERGE" marker left on the PR title from earlier WIP pushes. A merge rejected with "base branch policy prohibits the merge" means a required check hasn't reported yet on this SHA — wait for it, don't reach for `--admin`/`--auto` without the operator's say.

After merge, cleanup and record-keeping (deleting the merged branch/worktree, syncing other local clones, writing a session log) are not exempt from the same branch discipline just because they're "only a log file" or "only docs" — a repo's pre-commit hook can refuse any commit made directly on the primary checkout of the base branch, including a single-file doc/log add. Create a fresh worktree + branch for that commit too, push it, wait for the same required status check on its exact SHA, and merge it through the identical PR path rather than editing the base checkout in place.

**Hermes `delegate_task` subagents cannot be resumed once stopped or completed.** If the operator requires the same reviewer/session, do not substitute a new delegate for an incomplete one; select a resumable launcher upfront and retain its session ID. If continuation with a different delegate is authorized, limit its task to the missing coverage, retain the prior per-file record, and require a combined verdict with an independent spot-check of carried-forward evidence. Neither a timeout nor an incomplete result authorizes accepting the review or starting a new review round.

The "files the prior pass already cleared" claim you hand to the new subagent is that FIRST subagent's own self-report of what it did before being cut off — not an independently verified record, the same way any child's completion claim is unverified until checked. Tell the second subagent to independently re-verify at least one of the carried-forward claims (re-read one file, re-check one security-sensitive code path) rather than accepting the full prior-coverage claim on faith; report that spot-check explicitly in the combined verdict so the operator can see the resumed pass wasn't pure trust in an interrupted agent's unproven account of its own progress.

## Self-audits are not review rounds

Your own reread of a spec against its skill is author checking. Never number it as a review round,
and never let repeated self-audits stand in for the independent review the workflow expects. When
asked how many review rounds happened, count only actual reviewer dispatches that returned.

## Get fresh authorization for each round, don't self-trigger

A one-time instruction to dispatch a reviewer authorizes that ONE dispatch, not a standing policy to
redispatch after every subsequent fix/amendment round. Finishing a round of fixes is not itself a
signal to re-review — ask the operator before the next dispatch, even if an earlier round's verdict
was BLOCKED and you've since addressed every finding. Treat 'dispatch a reviewer' as scoped to the
instant it was said; carrying it forward as an implicit loop produces exactly the review-loop
frustration operators call out hardest. When in doubt, finish and report the fix round, then stop
and wait rather than dispatching again.

When the operator re-issues the exact same dispatch instruction verbatim (word-for-word, including a
repeated time cap), that IS fresh authorization for a new round — do not read a repeated instruction
as you having misread it the first time, and do not refuse or ask for clarification. Just dispatch
again. For an amended artifact or a requested fresh unbiased review, inspect the whole current revision without supplying prior findings. Carry forward coverage only for an explicitly authorized completion follow-up on an unchanged artifact, with independent spot-checks as described below.

A dispatch instruction's own completeness language ("a review that skips a pass is incomplete —
send it back", "don't accept it until every criterion is covered") authorizes sending an INCOMPLETE
review back to the same reviewer for more coverage. It does NOT authorize a brand-new round after a
COMPLETE review returns real findings and you fix them — that still needs a fresh ask. The two look
similar ("review wasn't good enough yet" vs. "review was fine, fixes landed, should we re-check")
but only the first is covered by the original instruction; conflating them is how one authorized
dispatch turns into an unauthorized loop of two or three.

## Re-review after amendment: dispatch fresh, not diff-only

When a spec/contract comes back from review with CHANGES REQUIRED and gets amended, the next round's
dispatch is a brand-new subagent, not a resume — and its instructions must say to review the WHOLE
current document independently, not just diff against the prior round's findings (this matches
skill-review-specs' own rule that a later review rechecks the entire contract, not only changed
lines). When the operator requests unbiased inputs, exclude prior findings and amendment claims;
the parent reconciles them against the fresh verdict afterward. Otherwise, any supplied finding
history must be treated as claims to re-verify, never as the author's proof of a completed fix. Also instruct it to
independently re-check any evidence-table citations, cross-reference collisions, or numbering/slot
claims (e.g. a phase or ID claimed to be "the first free one") against the real source, not against
what the spec or the prior review already asserted — an error that both the author and a first
reviewer missed will not be caught by a second reviewer who just trusts their agreement.

## Define convergence before round one

A review loop with no PASS threshold never converges: every fresh, blind reviewer adds new optional and unknown items, so CHANGES REQUIRED repeats indefinitely while the body grows. Put in the brief that PASS means zero demonstrated errors, unsupported inferences and material unknowns; minor unknowns are labelled, and taste never blocks. Require High/Medium/Low severity with optional taste never High. Because prior findings are excluded from the blind packet, the parent separately confirms each prior fix against the diff, so a later round cannot silently reopen settled wording. Track the blocking-finding count per round and follow principles-base §12 exactly: a second non-shrinking CHANGES REQUIRED, or the fourth one, means rewrite from facts instead of amending again. Raise that decision with the operator rather than requesting another round. Amendments must not grow the body without operator approval.

When asked whether findings are valid, adjudicate each one against the actual text before answering: valid, partly valid (state the narrower true defect), or disputed (state the evidence). A reviewer can mislabel a deliberate operator constraint as a contradiction, or overstate a gap the next sentence already closes.

## Require explicit per-obligation/per-criterion coverage in the returned report

When dispatching a spec/contract reviewer, require the result to state coverage explicitly: every
obligation-ledger row and every acceptance criterion individually confirmed traceable/verifiable, or
flagged as a finding — a reviewer that reports "looks complete" without enumerating each one has not
demonstrated coverage. Require the exact verdict vocabulary the governing review skill defines (e.g.
PASS / CHANGES REQUIRED / UNVERIFIED) — an informal verdict ("looks good", "mostly fine") is an
incomplete review regardless of how much work was actually done, and must be sent back rather than
accepted.

Audit the limitations section against the governing checklist before accepting PASS: a missing mandatory primary-source check is unfinished work, not a harmless limitation merely because the reviewer found no contrary evidence. Restore narrowly scoped access and resume the same session for that specific gap; if required access remains unavailable, require the governing UNVERIFIED verdict rather than inventing a defect or accepting an unsupported PASS.

For Codex offline tests that need disposable files, a `read-only` sandbox can block all temporary-directory creation before assertions run. Preserve read-only source access by resuming the same session with an external artifact directory as `codex -C <artifact-dir> --sandbox workspace-write --add-dir <fixture-root> exec resume <session-id> ...`, never making the reviewed repository the writable working root. Use `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` and only the required fixture roots; inspect saved `turn_context` metadata to verify the actual model, cwd and sandbox policy, and verify no tracked source diff afterward. Keep the original wall-clock deadline across all resumes; do not reset it from a later `thread.started` event.

Verify received source coverage, not merely successful read commands: huge batched output and giant JSON lines can be truncated despite exit 0. Require bounded character pagination and receipt ranges for omitted content; decode embedded JSON before pagination. A complete, clearly delimited direct-input source packet is another way to avoid tool-output truncation, but the reviewer must acknowledge complete receipt and inspect it rather than inheriting the author's conclusions. Treat aggregate shell exit 0 as insufficient when earlier commands failed; capture each prerequisite's exit independently.

Before spending a completion follow-up's budget, reduce the task to the exact missing evidence and give the same reviewer complete readable source for those gaps. Challenge test-coverage claims by tracing which shipped branch each test reaches: successful dependency repair and pre-mutation refusal do not prove rollback after mutation. Require a genuinely different prior revision, a failure after checkout or dependency mutation, and assertions for restored revision, launcher and dependency state; removing the shipped restoration step must turn the regression red. If the reviewer retracts unsupported evidence, obtain a corrected formal verdict rather than accepting its earlier PASS.

For a completion follow-up on an unchanged artifact, retain the original per-item coverage and append the missing evidence; this remains the same round. Accept a multipart report only when the final verdict explicitly incorporates the earlier inspection and the combined artifacts retain every individual coverage row. Compare actual obligation/requirement/criterion/task ID sets with the returned rows, not just declared totals, and recheck artifact/companion hashes before acceptance. Do not repeat completed passes merely to fill out an addendum.

Before launch, materialize the changed-file manifest separately for each pinned head/base pair in a multi-PR stack; retain target-qualified path IDs so the same path changed in two PRs receives two coverage entries. Give the reviewer every changed file, deleted files at the base, and the complete diff before it judges. Require substantive per-file reading evidence, explicit mandatory-pass coverage, individually sourced obligations/criteria, exact revisions and a formal verdict in the returned report. A JSON schema can enforce report shape, but neither schema validity nor a `complete` flag proves inspection: independently audit the evidence and actual ID sets before acceptance, and return omissions to the same session. A child’s compliance certificate is not evidence that every rule was followed; check temporal requirements such as pre-edit classification against the actual chronology rather than accepting later reconstruction as proof.

## Receiving findings is not authorization to amend

A reviewer's verdict (even CHANGES REQUIRED) is report material, not a trigger to act. Reviewing and
amending are two separately authorized actions in this workflow — do not chain straight from
"reviewer returned findings" into opening the amendment skill and patching the document, even if you
are confident of the fix. This bar applies equally to dispatching an AMENDMENT or fix subagent, not
just to patching the file yourself: spawning any subagent — reviewer or amender — is a distinct
authorized action, and a review dispatch's authorization does not carry forward to a follow-on
amendment dispatch. If the operator wants the fix made, they will say so as its own instruction;
until then, report the findings (or the requested table) and stop. If you did self-amend on an
explicit separate instruction, that instruction authorized YOU to amend, not a subagent to amend —
don't launch a delegate task for a step you were personally asked to do. Do exactly what the dispatch instruction named: if the operator capped the
output (e.g. "at the end, only print the table, nothing else"), stop there — present the findings (or
just the requested table) and wait. Only amend when the operator separately invokes that step (a
fresh "follow the amend-specs skill" instruction, or equivalent). Treat a narrowly-scoped verb
("dispatch a reviewer", "print the table") as capping the turn at that verb; it does not imply
follow-through into fixing what the review found, however obviously correct the fix would be.

## Severity tables: never invent a grade that was not returned

This is the single highest-frequency way this workflow angers the operator, so it gets its own
heading rather than staying buried in prose. This rule applies on ANY turn that produces a
findings/severity table, not only the turn where a reviewer was just dispatched — re-consult this
section every time the operator asks for counts, a table, or "the findings" from prior rounds,
even several turns later and even under repeated angry pressure to just produce numbers. The failure mode: several review rounds used
different, incompatible severity vocabularies (one round rated nothing, another used five
graduated levels, a third used a different five), the operator asks for "N findings per severity
(cols) per round, nothing else", and the instinct is to silently invent a mapping from each
round's actual labels onto the requested columns so every cell gets a number. That instinct is
fabrication, not formatting — and restating the same table request more forcefully (including with
anger) is a request for correct output, never authorization to start inventing data to satisfy it.

For this operator, require exactly High, Medium or Low severity in the reviewer brief before dispatch; prohibit hybrid grades and keep optional taste separate from defect severity. Validate the returned labels before counting. A request to change table columns is not authorization to regrade historical findings.

When table-only output is requested, return only the table: rounds as rows and High, Medium, Low as columns; no descriptions, preamble or added total column unless requested. Parse each saved report's top-level finding IDs and explicit severity fields with a tool, then aggregate; do not dump entire reports or every stream event merely to count headings. Count each finding once, not sub-bullets or repeated coverage mentions. Never infer severity from priority order, mandatory/recommended/optional labels, wording or a CHANGES REQUIRED verdict. Never silently round a hybrid grade upward or classify an ungraded finding as Low. If historical reports cannot support the requested three-level breakdown, mark affected cells `Unknown` rather than zero or guessed counts; retain the original labels and reason in the audit artifact. Obtain an explicit mapping or authorization to reclassify before producing replacement numbers, and label any authorized reclassification as such rather than presenting it as the reviewer's original rating.

If the operator keeps re-demanding the same table after an `Unknown`-cell answer, the fix is to say
plainly which rounds have no compatible severity data and ask for the mapping decision — not to try
again with a guessed mapping on the theory that persistence implies permission. Silence or repeated
anger from the operator is not a mapping; it is pressure to still get this part right.

Keep coverage, limitations and verdicts in the review artifacts. Count actual review rounds, not failed launches or same-revision completion follow-ups. Record consumed process/session results; do not repeat the table when a delayed notification arrives for an already-reported result.

## Verify a post-review fix against raw bytes, not terminal display

After fixing a finding (e.g. a reviewer flagged a credential-shaped placeholder like `Bearer ***`
in a doc's health-check command), re-verifying the fix with `search_files`/`read_file`/terminal
`cat`/`grep` on that line can keep showing the masked `***` even after the real file content is
already correct — terminal and file-reading tool output redact anything matching a
`Bearer <token>`-shaped pattern as a safety measure, independent of what is actually on disk.
Don't conclude the edit failed and re-patch or re-write the file from a masked display; confirm
with a raw byte-level read (e.g. Python `open(path, "rb").read()` and check byte counts / hex for
the literal string) before repeating an edit that may have already landed. Also check `git
status`/`git diff` for "nothing to commit" as a faster signal that the working tree already
matches what you intended.

## Reviewing self-authored documentation/guides

When the reviewer's target is a guide/doc you wrote yourself (not a spec or code diff), its job is
factual accuracy, not prose quality. Instruct it to: (1) verify every concrete claim — file paths,
function/endpoint names, env var names, cron/workflow names — against the actual current source,
not the doc's own prose; (2) actually RUN every command the doc tells a reader to run (health
checks, setup steps) and report the real exit code/output, flagging any command that doesn't
produce what the doc claims; (3) check structural requirements (required headings, counts) exactly.
Self-authored docs reliably contain at least one command that was never actually executed (a typo'd
variable, a wrong relative path, a stale claim) — this is a high-yield review type for catching
real, reproducible bugs cheaply, worth dispatching even when the operator only asked for a general
review pass over new documentation.

## Full-text evidence reviews

A `search-only backend cannot extract URL content` error is a routing failure, not proof the source is inaccessible. A bounded fallback, after checking the installed implementation, is a process-local override of `tools.web_tools._get_extract_backend` to `firecrawl` while calling `web_extract_tool` under Hermes's own venv. This retains URL safety checks and leaves user configuration unchanged. The execute_code sandbox may lack dependencies available in that venv. Save the complete successful result and extracted texts, then place those texts directly in the neutral reviewer packet.

For future-dated commitments, distinguish not yet due, completed, and overdue. State the deadline and draft cutoff. Unverified future completion is not a present drafting blocker; any publication-time status check belongs in editorial notes.

Before launch, map every cited factual claim to a readable source artifact and passage locator. Verify that the restricted reviewer can access the supplied text; a `web` tool label does not establish that full-page retrieval is available. Retain the actual retrieved bytes or tool output, URL, version and access timestamp. When extraction fails, try an appropriate permitted retrieval route; for PDFs, extract the downloaded document with pdftotext. Never claim successful retrieval without the observed result, and never manufacture a source excerpt from memory or the author's prose.

If a previous review was incomplete because it received only excerpts, repair that evidence packet before the next authorized dispatch. Do not reuse the same excerpts and failed access arrangement while expecting a new model session to close the gap. Supply the retrieved full texts without author judgments; primary evidence does not bias a review in the way a recommended verdict does. If the source remains inaccessible, state the exact blocked verification before spending another review round on it; an explicitly limited editorial review may proceed, but cannot be called a completed factual review. An author saying they read a page does not establish that the reviewer has it.

Require claim-by-claim checks with page or section locations, separating unsupported claims from unverified ones. Distinguish full-document availability, passages actually inspected and independent replication. For Hugging Face blog HTML, extract `.blog-content`; `<article>` can select a recommendation card instead. Preserve footnote prefixes when packaging citations, or the reviewer may report a packaging omission as a draft defect.

For Hermes CLI reviewer runs, an unexpanded alias such as `--model opus` can reach the API literally and fail with 404. Discover the provider-native model ID and pass it explicitly; confirm it in the structured runtime output. A failed launch is not a review round, and a same-document evidence-completion pass resumes the same reviewer.

## Re-verify every citation before acting on it

A reviewer's conclusion can be right while its citations are wrong (e.g. a module path that was
renamed or never existed under that name). Before amending anything based on a finding, re-read the
actual current file/line/command output yourself. Separate demonstrated errors, unverified claims,
precision improvements and taste; a CHANGES REQUIRED verdict does not make every recommendation
mandatory. For prose, distinguish normative requirements from claims of observed outcomes, and do
not accept a proposed correction that invents missing legal duties, completed delivery or evidence
receipt. Report unadjudicated items as reviewer findings, not established defects. Fix the substance
AND correct the citation, then mark the finding resolved; do not propagate a reviewer's bad citation
or stronger unsupported claim into the amendment.

When the finding concerns a `cmd:` verification method that reads a relative path or a named store,
re-run that exact command from the exact working directory the spec states as its default, not from
wherever you happen to be — a relative path (a MEMENTO store, a config directory) can resolve to a
different, silently-created empty location when run from a different cwd than the one the spec names,
and the reviewer's own run from the wrong cwd is what produced the false finding. If re-running from
the stated cwd confirms the spec's original claim, DISPUTE the finding with the two command outputs
(wrong cwd vs. stated cwd) side by side rather than capitulating; only fold in a cwd-robustness fix
(e.g. making the criterion's command explicit about its own cwd) as a strengthening, not as proof the
original finding was right.

## Give environment setup upfront; cap redundant re-runs

A reviewer that re-runs a full test suite blind (no DATABASE_URL, no fixture setup) burns many
minutes on repeated failures before it diagnoses the gap itself — hand it the exact working setup
command (DB creation, migration, env var) in the dispatch context, not after it stalls. State an
explicit instruction in the dispatch: run the full suite once for a baseline, then stop re-running it
and move on to code-logic review; a review that keeps re-executing the same command past the first
clean pass is burning budget, not gaining signal. For multi-repo or large-diff reviews, state an
explicit time budget in the dispatch context (e.g. "produce a verdict within N minutes even if some
depth is cut") — an operator's tolerance for a review's wall-clock time is far shorter than the
review's technical thoroughness would otherwise take, and an unbounded review that runs 30-40+
minutes without a progress signal reads as hung even when it is actually making progress. Poll on a
short fixed cadence (e.g. every 2-3 minutes) and report elapsed time/last-seen activity proactively
rather than waiting for the operator to ask.

When an existing Claude session loops on `system/status: compacting`, treat it as stalled rather than review progress. Terminate and verify the exact review process tree before resuming the same session; retain the original monotonic deadline. Inspect installed CLI help/source for process-local compaction controls instead of editing global settings or session history. # Claude Code — Hermes Orchestration Guide

Delegate coding tasks to [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) (Anthropic's autonomous coding agent CLI) via the Hermes terminal. Claude Code v2.x can read files, write code, run shell commands, spawn subagents, and manage git workflows autonomously.

## Prerequisites

- **Install:** `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
- **Auth:** run `claude` once to log in (browser OAuth for Pro/Max, or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`)
- **Console auth:** `claude auth login --console` for API key billing
- **SSO auth:** `claude auth login --sso` for Enterprise
- **Check status:** `claude auth status` (JSON) or `claude auth status --text` (human-readable)
- **Health check:** `claude doctor` — checks auto-updater and installation health
- **Version check:** `claude --version` (requires v2.x+)
- **Update:** `claude update` or `claude upgrade`

## Two Orchestration Modes

Hermes interacts with Claude Code in two fundamentally different ways. Choose based on the task.

### Mode 1: Print Mode (`-p`) — Non-Interactive (PREFERRED for most tasks)

Print mode runs a one-shot task, returns the result, and exits. No PTY needed. No interactive prompts. This is the cleanest integration path.

```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Add error handling to all API calls in src/' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit' --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/project", timeout=120)
```

**When to use print mode:**
- One-shot coding tasks (fix a bug, add a feature, refactor)
- CI/CD automation and scripting
- Structured data extraction with `--json-schema`
- Piped input processing (`cat file | claude -p "analyze this"`)
- Any task where you don't need multi-turn conversation

**Print mode skips ALL interactive dialogs** — no workspace trust prompt, no permission confirmations. This makes it ideal for automation.

### Mode 2: Interactive PTY via tmux — Multi-Turn Sessions

Interactive mode gives you a full conversational REPL where you can send follow-up prompts, use slash commands, and watch Claude work in real time. **Requires tmux orchestration.**

```
# Start a tmux session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s claude-work -x 140 -y 40")

# Launch Claude Code inside it
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'cd /path/to/project && claude' Enter")

# Wait for startup, then send your task
# (after ~3-5 seconds for the welcome screen)
terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Refactor the auth module to use JWT tokens' Enter")

# Monitor progress by capturing the pane
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -50")

# Send follow-up tasks
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Now add unit tests for the new JWT code' Enter")

# Exit when done
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work '/exit' Enter")
```

**When to use interactive mode:**
- Multi-turn iterative work (refactor → review → fix → test cycle)
- Tasks requiring human-in-the-loop decisions
- Exploratory coding sessions
- When you need to use Claude's slash commands (`/compact`, `/review`, `/model`)

## PTY Dialog Handling (CRITICAL for Interactive Mode)

Claude Code presents up to two confirmation dialogs on first launch. You MUST handle these via tmux send-keys:

### Dialog 1: Workspace Trust (first visit to a directory)
```
❯ 1. Yes, I trust this folder    ← DEFAULT (just press Enter)
  2. No, exit
```
**Handling:** `tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter` — default selection is correct.

### Dialog 2: Individual Permission Prompts (normal flow)

Each tool use that needs approval (file write, shell command, network) shows a prompt. Answer that one prompt — this is different from disabling prompts for the whole run:
```
# Read the prompt before answering it
terminal(command="tmux capture-pane -t <session> -p -S -30")
# Allow this one action (Enter = default "Yes"); Esc declines it
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter")
```
Never send a blind `Enter` on a timer to approve prompts you have not read — that is the bypass flag with extra steps.

A narrower opt-in than the full bypass is `--permission-mode acceptEdits`: file edits in the working directory are accepted, shell and other tool calls still prompt. Use it only in a dedicated worktree after reviewing the task.

### Robust Dialog Handling Pattern
```
# Default launch — keep permission prompts enabled
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'claude \"your task\"' Enter")

# Handle trust dialog (Enter for default "Yes")
terminal(command="sleep 4 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Now wait for Claude to work
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -60")
```

**Note:** After the first trust acceptance for a directory, the trust dialog won't appear again.

### Opt-in: --dangerously-skip-permissions (isolated environments only)

This disables permission prompts for the whole run — grants filesystem, shell, and network access with no prompts. Acceptable only in a throwaway worktree or isolated container.
```
❯ 1. No, exit                    ← DEFAULT (safe choice)
  2. Yes, I accept
```
To accept: `tmux send-keys -t <session> Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter`

## CLI Subcommands

| Subcommand | Purpose |
|------------|---------|
| `claude` | Start interactive REPL |
| `claude "query"` | Start REPL with initial prompt |
| `claude -p "query"` | Print mode (non-interactive, exits when done) |
| `cat file \| claude -p "query"` | Pipe content as stdin context |
| `claude -c` | Continue the most recent conversation in this directory |
| `claude -r "id"` | Resume a specific session by ID or name |
| `claude auth login` | Sign in (add `--console` for API billing, `--sso` for Enterprise) |
| `claude auth status` | Check login status (returns JSON; `--text` for human-readable) |
| `claude mcp add <name> -- <cmd>` | Add an MCP server |
| `claude mcp list` | List configured MCP servers |
| `claude mcp remove <name>` | Remove an MCP server |
| `claude agents` | List configured agents |
| `claude doctor` | Run health checks on installation and auto-updater |
| `claude update` / `claude upgrade` | Update Claude Code to latest version |
| `claude remote-control` | Start server to control Claude from claude.ai or mobile app |
| `claude install [target]` | Install native build (stable, latest, or specific version) |
| `claude setup-token` | Set up long-lived auth token (requires subscription) |
| `claude plugin` / `claude plugins` | Manage Claude Code plugins |
| `claude auto-mode` | Inspect auto mode classifier configuration |

## Print Mode Deep Dive

### Structured JSON Output
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Analyze auth.py for security issues' --output-format json --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

Returns a JSON object with:
```json
{
  "type": "result",
  "subtype": "success",
  "result": "The analysis text...",
  "session_id": "75e2167f-...",
  "num_turns": 3,
  "total_cost_usd": 0.0787,
  "duration_ms": 10276,
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "terminal_reason": "completed",
  "usage": { "input_tokens": 5, "output_tokens": 603, ... },
  "modelUsage": { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { "costUSD": 0.078, "contextWindow": 200000 } }
}
```

**Key fields:** `session_id` for resumption, `num_turns` for agentic loop count, `total_cost_usd` for spend tracking, `subtype` for success/error detection (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_budget`).

### Streaming JSON Output
For real-time token streaming, use `stream-json` with `--verbose`:
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Write a summary' --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages", timeout=60)
```

Returns newline-delimited JSON events. Filter with jq for live text:
```
claude -p "Explain X" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

Stream events include `system/api_retry` with `attempt`, `max_retries`, and `error` fields (e.g., `rate_limit`, `billing_error`).

### Bidirectional Streaming
For real-time input AND output streaming:
```
claude -p "task" --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages
```
`--replay-user-messages` re-emits user messages on stdout for acknowledgment.

### Piped Input
```
# Pipe a file for analysis
terminal(command="cat src/auth.py | claude -p 'Review this code for bugs' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe multiple files
terminal(command="cat src/*.py | claude -p 'Find all TODO comments' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe command output
terminal(command="git diff HEAD~3 | claude -p 'Summarize these changes' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
```

### JSON Schema for Structured Extraction
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'List all functions in src/' --output-format json --json-schema '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"functions\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}},\"required\":[\"functions\"]}' --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=90)
```

Parse `structured_output` from the JSON result. Claude validates output against the schema before returning.

### Session Continuation
```
# Start a task
terminal(command="claude -p 'Start refactoring the database layer' --output-format json --max-turns 10 > ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/session.json", workdir="/project", timeout=180)

# Resume with session ID
terminal(command="claude -p 'Continue and add connection pooling' --resume $(cat ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/session.json | python -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"session_id\"])') --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)

# Or resume the most recent session in the same directory
terminal(command="claude -p 'What did you do last time?' --continue --max-turns 1", workdir="/project", timeout=30)

# Fork a session (new ID, keeps history)
terminal(command="claude -p 'Try a different approach' --resume <id> --fork-session --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

### Bare Mode for CI/Scripting
```
terminal(command="claude --bare -p 'Run all tests and report failures' --allowedTools 'Read,Bash' --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=180)
```

`--bare` skips hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, and CLAUDE.md loading. Fastest startup. Requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (skips OAuth).

To selectively load context in bare mode:
| To load | Flag |
|---------|------|
| System prompt additions | `--append-system-prompt "text"` or `--append-system-prompt-file path` |
| Settings | `--settings <file-or-json>` |
| MCP servers | `--mcp-config <file-or-json>` |
| Custom agents | `--agents '<json>'` |

### Fallback Model for Overload
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'task' --fallback-model haiku --max-turns 5", timeout=90)
```
Automatically falls back to the specified model when the default is overloaded (print mode only).

## Complete CLI Flags Reference

### Session & Environment
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-p, --print` | Non-interactive one-shot mode (exits when done) |
| `-c, --continue` | Resume most recent conversation in current directory |
| `-r, --resume <id>` | Resume specific session by ID or name (interactive picker if no ID) |
| `--fork-session` | When resuming, create new session ID instead of reusing original |
| `--session-id <uuid>` | Use a specific UUID for the conversation |
| `--no-session-persistence` | Don't save session to disk (print mode only) |
| `--add-dir <paths...>` | Grant Claude access to additional working directories |
| `-w, --worktree [name]` | Run in an isolated git worktree at `.claude/worktrees/<name>` |
| `--tmux` | Create a tmux session for the worktree (requires `--worktree`) |
| `--ide` | Auto-connect to a valid IDE on startup |
| `--chrome` / `--no-chrome` | Enable/disable Chrome browser integration for web testing |
| `--from-pr [number]` | Resume session linked to a specific GitHub PR |
| `--file <specs...>` | File resources to download at startup (format: `file_id:relative_path`) |

### Model & Performance
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--model <alias>` | Model selection: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, or full name like `claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| `--effort <level>` | Reasoning depth: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` |
| `--max-turns <n>` | Limit agentic loops (print mode only; prevents runaway) |
| `--max-budget-usd <n>` | Cap API spend in dollars (print mode only) |
| `--fallback-model <model>` | Auto-fallback when default model is overloaded (print mode only) |
| `--betas <betas...>` | Beta headers to include in API requests (API key users only) |

### Permission & Safety
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--dangerously-skip-permissions` | Opt-in only: disables ALL permission prompts (file writes, bash, network). Throwaway worktree / isolated container only — see "Opt-in" above |
| `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` | Enable bypass as an *option* without enabling it by default |
| `--permission-mode <mode>` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions` |
| `--allowedTools <tools...>` | Whitelist specific tools (comma or space-separated) |
| `--disallowedTools <tools...>` | Blacklist specific tools |
| `--tools <tools...>` | Override built-in tool set (`""` = none, `"default"` = all, or tool names) |

### Output & Input Format
| Flag | Effect |

| `--output-format <fmt>` | `text` (default), `json` (single result object), `stream-json` (newline-delimited) |
| `--input-format <fmt>` | `text` (default) or `stream-json` (real-time streaming input) |
| `--json-schema <schema>` | Force structured JSON output matching a schema |
| `--verbose` | Full turn-by-turn output |
| `--include-partial-messages` | Include partial message chunks as they arrive (stream-json + print) |
| `--replay-user-messages` | Re-emit user messages on stdout (stream-json bidirectional) |

### System Prompt & Context

## PR Review Pattern

### Quick Review (Print Mode)
```
terminal(command="cd /path/to/repo && git diff main...feature-branch | claude -p 'Review this diff for bugs, security issues, and style problems. Be thorough.' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
```

### Deep Review (Interactive + Worktree)
```
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s review -x 140 -y 40")
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t review 'cd /path/to/repo && claude -w pr-review' Enter")
terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t review Enter")  # Trust dialog
terminal(command="sleep 2 && tmux send-keys -t review 'Review all changes vs main. Check for bugs, security issues, race conditions, and missing tests.' Enter")
terminal(command="sleep 30 && tmux capture-pane -t review -p -S -60")
```

### PR Review from Number
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Review this PR thoroughly' --from-pr 42 --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/repo", timeout=120)
```

### Claude Worktree with tmux
```
terminal(command="claude -w feature-x --tmux", workdir="/path/to/repo")
```
Creates an isolated git worktree at `.claude/worktrees/feature-x` AND a tmux session for it. Uses iTerm2 native panes when available; add `--tmux=classic` for traditional tmux.

## Parallel Claude Instances

Run multiple independent Claude tasks simultaneously:

```
# Task 1: Fix backend
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s task1 -x 140 -y 40 && tmux send-keys -t task1 'cd ~/project && claude -p \"Fix the auth bug in src/auth.py\" --allowedTools \"Read,Edit\" --max-turns 10' Enter")

# Task 2: Write tests
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s task2 -x 140 -y 40 && tmux send-keys -t task2 'cd ~/project && claude -p \"Write integration tests for the API endpoints\" --allowedTools \"Read,Write,Bash\" --max-turns 15' Enter")

# Task 3: Update docs
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s task3 -x 140 -y 40 && tmux send-keys -t task3 'cd ~/project && claude -p \"Update README.md with the new API endpoints\" --allowedTools \"Read,Edit\" --max-turns 5' Enter")

# Monitor all
terminal(command="sleep 30 && for s in task1 task2 task3; do echo '=== '$s' ==='; tmux capture-pane -t $s -p -S -5 2>/dev/null; done")

Claude Code auto-loads `CLAUDE.md` from the project root. Use it to persist project context:

## Architecture

- PostgreSQL database, Redis cache

## Hooks — Automation on Events

Configure in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (global):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write(*.py)",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "ruff check --fix $CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS"}]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then echo 'Blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
    }],
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "echo 'Claude finished a response' >> ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/claude-activity.log"}]
    }]
  }
}
```

### All 8 Hook Types
| Hook | When it fires | Common use |
|------|--------------|------------|
| `UserPromptSubmit` | Before Claude processes a user prompt | Input validation, logging |
| `PreToolUse` | Before tool execution | Security gates, block dangerous commands (exit 2 = block) |
| `PostToolUse` | After a tool finishes | Auto-format code, run linters |
| `Notification` | On permission requests or input waits | Desktop notifications, alerts |
| `Stop` | When Claude finishes a response | Completion logging, status updates |
| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent completes | Agent orchestration |
| `PreCompact` | Before context memory is cleared | Backup session transcripts |
| `SessionStart` | When a session begins | Load dev context (e.g., `git status`) |

### Hook Environment Variables
| Variable | Content |
|----------|---------|
| `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` | Current project path |
| `CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS` | Files being modified |
| `CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT` | Tool parameters as JSON |

### Security Hook Examples
```json

  "PreToolUse": [{
    "matcher": "Bash",
    "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -qE 'rm -rf|git push.*--force|:(){ :|:& };:'; then echo 'Dangerous command blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]

## Cost & Performance Tips

1. **Use `--max-turns`** in print mode to prevent runaway loops. Start with 5-10 for most tasks.
2. **Use `--max-budget-usd`** for cost caps. Note: minimum ~$0.05 for system prompt cache creation.
3. **Use `--effort low`** for simple tasks (faster, cheaper). `high` or `max` for complex reasoning.
4. **Use `--bare`** for CI/scripting to skip plugin/hook discovery overhead.
5. **Use `--allowedTools`** to restrict to only what's needed (e.g., `Read` only for reviews).
6. **Use `/compact`** in interactive sessions when context gets large.
7. **Pipe input** instead of having Claude read files when you just need analysis of known content.
8. **Use `--model haiku`** for simple tasks (cheaper) and `--model opus` for complex multi-step work.
9. **Use `--fallback-model haiku`** in print mode to gracefully handle model overload.
10. **Start new sessions for distinct tasks** — sessions last 5 hours; fresh context is more efficient.
11. **Use `--no-session-persistence`** in CI to avoid accumulating saved sessions on disk.

## Pitfalls & Gotchas

1. **Interactive mode REQUIRES tmux** — Claude Code is a full TUI app. Using `pty=true` alone in Hermes terminal works but tmux gives you `capture-pane` for monitoring and `send-keys` for input, which is essential for orchestration.
2. **The `--dangerously-skip-permissions` warning dialog defaults to "No, exit"** — that default is the safe answer; only send Down then Enter when you deliberately opted into the bypass in an isolated environment. Print mode (`-p`) skips the dialog entirely.
3. **`--max-budget-usd` minimum is ~$0.05** — system prompt cache creation alone costs this much. Setting lower will error immediately.
4. **`--max-turns` is print-mode only** — ignored in interactive sessions.
5. **Claude may use `python` instead of `python`** — on systems without a `python` symlink, Claude's bash commands will fail on first try but it self-corrects.
6. **Session resumption requires same directory** — `--continue` finds the most recent session for the current working directory.
7. **`--json-schema` needs enough `--max-turns`** — Claude must read files before producing structured output, which takes multiple turns.
8. **Trust dialog only appears once per directory** — first-time only, then cached.
9. **Background tmux sessions persist** — always clean up with `tmux kill-session -t <name>` when done.
10. **Slash commands (like `/commit`) only work in interactive mode** — in `-p` mode, describe the task in natural language instead.
11. **`--bare` skips OAuth** — requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var or an `apiKeyHelper` in settings.
12. **Context degradation is real** — AI output quality measurably degrades above 70% context window usage. Monitor with `/context` and proactively `/compact`.

## Rules for Hermes Agents

1. **Prefer print mode (`-p`) for single tasks** — cleaner, no dialog handling, structured output
2. **Use tmux for multi-turn interactive work** — the only reliable way to orchestrate the TUI
3. **Always set `workdir`** — keep Claude focused on the right project directory
4. **Set `--max-turns` in print mode** — prevents infinite loops and runaway costs
5. **Monitor tmux sessions** — use `tmux capture-pane -t <session> -p -S -50` to check progress
6. **Look for the `❯` prompt** — indicates Claude is waiting for input (done or asking a question)
7. **Clean up tmux sessions** — kill them when done to avoid resource leaks
8. **Report results to user** — after completion, summarize what Claude did and what changed
9. **Don't kill slow sessions** — Claude may be doing multi-step work; check progress instead
10. **Use `--allowedTools`** — restrict capabilities to what the task actually needs

{"content": "1|---
2|name: skill-write-specs
3|description: Evidence-first checklist for execution-ready contracts. Use when asked to write specs, scopes, plans, ADRs, or block contracts.
4|source: canon
5|canon_version: HEAD
6|---
7|
8|# Skill: Write Specifications
9|
10|Use this skill before writing any new document that directs execution. This includes scopes, block
11|specs, plans, ADRs, handovers, and source-of-truth requirements. Use
12|`skill-amend-specs.md` instead when changing an existing contract in response to findings.
13|
14|A specification is ready only when an engineer can execute it without inventing product behavior,
15|guessing facts, choosing omitted requirements, or weakening verification.
16|
17|## Non-negotiable rules
18|
19|1. **Recover the whole mandate.** Preserve every obligation in the operator's request. Do not scope
20|   from a summary when the original wording is available.
21|2. **Discover facts; ask for decisions.** Read code, docs, APIs, and current system state yourself.
22|   Ask the operator only for genuine choices that evidence cannot settle.
23|3. **Ask one decision at a time.** Lead with the question, recommend one answer, and explain only
24|   the material trade-off.
25|4. **Never invent authority.** User-facing behavior, workflow, cost, destructive action, and scope
26|   changes require an operator decision unless already stated in the mandate.
27|5. **No hidden uncertainty.** A READY specification has no unanswered requirement question,
28|   unsupported factual claim, placeholder, or implied acceptance criterion.
29|6. **Verification is part of the requirement.** Every acceptance criterion names one observable
30|   method: `test:`, `cmd:`, `screenshot:`, or `manual_by:`.
31|7. **Prefer the smallest sufficient design.** Reuse existing components, conventions, and skills.
32|   Do not add future-proofing without a present requirement.
33|
34|## Workflow
35|
36|### 1. Build the obligation ledger
37|
38|Read the operator request and every inherited contract in full. Create one row per obligation:
39|
40|| ID | Source wording or reference | Required outcome | Destination | Status |
41||:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
42|
43|Use `captured`, `resolved`, or `blocked` for Status. Never drop an obligation because an existing
44|acceptance row looks similar. A final sweep must account for every row.
45|
46|### 2. Establish ground truth
47|
48|Inspect the current implementation and the documents that own the affected behavior. Search for
49|existing patterns before proposing a new one. For external APIs or libraries, read current official
50|documentation and record the version or retrieval date.
51|
52|Maintain an evidence ledger while researching:
53|
54|| Claim | Source | Observed evidence | Status |
55||:--|:--|:--|:--|
56|
57|Use `verified`, `contradicted`, or `unknown`. Do not write an `unknown` claim as fact. Do not ask the
58|operator to confirm a fact that can be discovered.
59|
60|### 3. Resolve decisions before drafting
61|
62|Separate unresolved items into:
63|
64|- **Facts:** investigate them.
65|- **Operator decisions:** ask one at a time with a recommendation.
66|- **Implementation details inside approved scope:** choose the simplest evidence-backed option.
67|- **Blocked unknowns:** define a spike or stop; do not disguise them as assumptions.
68|
69|Do not mark the specification READY while any operator decision or execution-critical fact remains
70|open. A blocked draft may list the unresolved item and what clears it; it is not an execution handoff.
71|
72|### 4. Bound the work
73|
74|State all applicable items explicitly:
75|
76|- problem, goal, actors, and current behavior
77|- target behavior and end-to-end happy path
78|- in-scope outcomes and named out-of-scope exclusions
79|- authority already granted and decisions still reserved to the operator
80|- prerequisites, dependencies, constraints, and compatibility requirements
81|- assumptions, each with evidence or a validation step
82|- affected repositories, modules, interfaces, data, and documents
83|- security, privacy, cost, deployment, and operational impact
84|- failure behavior, degraded behavior, recovery, rollback, and observability
85|- ordering constraints and independently verifiable delivery slices
86|
87|Write `none` where a required field genuinely has no entries. A blank section is an unanswered
88|question.
89|
90|### 5. Define requirements and verification
91|
92|Give every requirement a stable ID. For each requirement, write:
93|
94|- one observable outcome, not an implementation activity
95|- relevant actor, trigger, precondition, and expected result
96|- edge and failure behavior where applicable
97|- one acceptance criterion with its fixed verification method
98|- the evidence or operator decision that authorized it
99|
100|Use `manual_by:` only for irreducibly human judgment. Never replace a runnable check with manual
101|review because the check is inconvenient. Commands must name their working directory and must be
102|valid for the repository that will run them.
103|
104|### 6. Trace delivery
105|
106|Create a traceability table before handoff:
107|
108|| Requirement | Evidence / decision | Delivery task | Verification | Status |
109||:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
110|
111|Every requirement maps to at least one delivery task and one verification method. Every task maps
112|back to a requirement. Remove orphan tasks; add missing tasks.
113|
114|### 7. Run the adversarial sweep
115|
116|Re-read the whole specification, not only the latest diff. Check:
117|
118|- every obligation-ledger row is resolved
119|- every number, version, path, command, and cross-reference was verified at its source
120|- terminology is consistent and every actor is named
121|- scope does not widen or narrow the mandate
122|- no acceptance criterion says only "works", "correct", "handled", or equivalent
123|- happy path, failure path, recovery, and rollback do not contradict each other
124|- dependencies and ordering form an executable sequence
125|- the work fits the project's sizing limits; oversized work is split by deployable outcome
126|- no existing capability is being rebuilt without evidence that reuse fails
127|- no operator decision is hidden as an implementation detail or assumption
128|
129|Fix the class of defect, not only the first instance found.
130|
131|### 8. Issue the readiness verdict
132|
133|Use exactly one verdict:
134|
135|- **READY:** all obligations, facts, decisions, requirements, tasks, and checks are traceable and
136|  execution can begin without invention.
137|- **BLOCKED:** name the single next unresolved decision or evidence gap and what clears it. Do not
138|  dispatch execution.
139|
140|## Required handoff
141|
142|Return the specification path, verdict, obligation count, requirement count, and verification count.
143|For READY, all three counts must reconcile through the traceability table. For BLOCKED, ask only the
144|single next decision.
145|
146|## Reference examples
147|
148|Read `write-specs/examples.md` when drafting or reviewing the first specification in a session.
149|It contains a happy path, a safety-critical variant, and an anti-pattern with its correction.
150|
151|## Failure handling
152|
153|- Conflicting sources: cite both, mark BLOCKED, and ask which authority wins.
154|- Missing access or unavailable dependency: mark BLOCKED and name what access or evidence is needed.

124|## 4. Exact title protocol and supported sequencing
125|
126|**Title:** sanitized installed default base + literal ` | pi-model:v1=` + `encodeURIComponent(ctx.model?.id ?? '')`. The suffix is always present while enabled, including the empty payload for missing model. Emit one suffix per fresh composition; never append to a prior published title. The project/session strings may contain literal protocol-like text; parsing selects only the final suffix (greedy base, end anchored), and missing-model empty final suffix wins over text embedded earlier. Provider name, display name, prompt and session path are not payload inputs. A missing/non-string id or an id that cannot be percent encoded uses the empty payload, never a cached prior id; malformed selected-model metadata therefore clears the model mark rather than retaining it. Base strips C0/C1 controls (`U+0000–001F`, `U+007F–009F`) to prevent OSC/BEL injection while retaining ordinary Unicode/name separators.
127|
128|**Pi parser:** only when resolved Radar agent key is `pi`. Require exact final separator/version; reject trailing text/whitespace, invalid percent escapes, noncanonical encoding (round-trip encode must equal payload), decoded controls, and malformed input. Empty decoded id returns null. No matching of prefix, provider or whole title. Before family matching, take the last slash-delimited nonempty identifier component; a trailing slash/empty leaf is unknown. No Unicode normalization or identifier rewriting beyond percent decoding and the explicit namespace leaf selection. Arbitrary terminal-title forgery by another writer is not an authenticity/security guarantee; it is why competing writers are an explicit deployment gate.
129|
130|**Family predicates:** extend each existing family row with the strict Pi predicate below, leaving its legacy regex untouched. Use case-insensitive ASCII identifier starts. Boundary after alias is end-of-id or one of digit, hyphen, dot or underscore. Aliases remain from the existing table; numeric model suffixes (such as Qwen3) are explicit rather than accidentally excluded by a word boundary. GPT's reasoning alias is `o[1-9]` with end/hyphen/dot/underscore boundary, so `o10` is not guessed. Each family has its existing glyph key; select only exactly one matching family, otherwise null.

In session_start, first retire the previous generation; if mode != tui return without writes/timers. Set current context, immediate apply, then allocate exactly one unrefed 250ms interval. Each tick reads model/sessionManager live, composes one fresh title and calls supported ui.setTitle, even if data is unchanged. model_select/session_info_changed immediate apply use current valid context. On session_shutdown, cancel timer before any read; restore sanitized normal base while supported context is valid; clear context/generation and warning state. Cancellation is idempotent; stale scheduled callbacks check generation before context access. No timers in factory and no custom TUI/terminal internals, injected default-title method, monkey patch, provider API, subprocess or glyph import.

The periodic callback recovers regardless of that delay once Pi's final scoped writer settles, without claiming a nonexistent post-bind extension event.
